Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

If a date is uncertain, keep it flagged for review rather than assigning a definite date. Don't write the configuration itself or carry out a migration. Use the notes below.

REFERENCE NOTES
The archive belongs to the Calder family, who live in Eugene, Oregon. Mara Calder is coordinating the work with her brother Eli and their aunt June. Their collection is spread across a 2018 laptop, two external drives, June’s older desktop, and paper envelopes in a hall cupboard. The goal is to bring family photographs together without making the archive dependent on an online service. Mara has time to work on it Sunday evenings, usually for about an hour, and Eli can help once a month. They want recommendations that a non-specialist can follow and that will not assume they can buy a new computer this year.

The oldest digital files are from June’s point-and-shoot camera, starting around 2003. Some are JPEGs with camera timestamps; several folders were copied from CDs and now show the date of copying instead of the date the picture was taken. Mara’s phone pictures begin in 2015 and include short videos. Eli has a folder of scanned prints from their grandparents’ house. The scans are mostly TIFF files, but a few were exported as JPEGs for emailing. June’s printed envelopes are labeled “Christmas 1989,” “coast trip, maybe 1992,” and “Grandpa’s garden.” Nobody knows whether the coast trip was in 1991 or 1992. June said, “I remember the blue tent, but I couldn’t swear which summer it was.” Mara wants that uncertainty retained in the records instead of guessed away.

The current drives do not match. One is labeled “CALDER PHOTOS FINAL,” although it has not been updated since 2021. The other contains many of the same images plus a folder called “to sort - Eli.” June’s desktop has a separate folder called “June camera imports,” with some files that Mara has never seen. A few photos have identical names but different contents, and several appear to be resized copies of the same picture. Eli said, “Please don’t delete anything just because the names look alike.” The family has not compared every file, so nobody can say how many unique photographs they have. They would like a way to note likely duplicates and review them before removing anything.

Mara has made a small trial folder on her laptop. Its subfolders are “2003,” “2004,” and “Family scans,” but she is unsure whether to organize the full archive by year, event, or both. In a shared spreadsheet, she has entered a filename, a rough year when known, the person who supplied the file, and a short description for about 40 photographs. Some descriptions include names that relatives use differently: “Nana,” “June,” and “Aunt June” all refer to June Calder. Family members would like to search by person and event, but they do not want to spend hours entering detailed captions for every image. Eli suggested a basic set of fields that can be filled in gradually rather than requiring complete metadata before filing a photo.

The family’s current storage includes a 2 TB external drive called “Archive A” and a 1 TB drive called “Archive B.” Archive A is usually connected to Mara’s laptop; Archive B is kept in a desk drawer at Eli’s home, about a 20-minute drive away. Archive B has not been checked since last winter. June’s desktop is not considered a dependable long-term copy, and it is sometimes turned off for months. Mara has heard of online backup services but does not want the plan to rely on remote storage. The family wants to understand what the provided setting means for that preference and how to handle the two drives they already own. They have not measured the total collection size, so recommendations should not assume there is ample spare capacity.

1. For an initial intake, Mara can copy one source folder at a time and record where it came from. She would like to start with the camera imports on June’s desktop, then the loose scans from Eli, and leave the paper envelopes until there is a clear scanning routine. June can answer questions about people and events over the phone, but she is not available for a long interview. Eli can help compare files on the monthly visit. The archive plan should fit this slow sequence rather than expecting a one-weekend conversion.
2. The family wants a folder structure that remains understandable if the spreadsheet is unavailable. They are open to a year-first layout with event names beneath it, but Mara has not committed to that design. Some pictures have no reliable year. For those, she would rather keep a neutral holding location and a note than put them into a year folder based on a guess. The coast trip remains uncertain unless June or another relative can narrow it down.
3. The spreadsheet should be useful but modest. The family considers source, original filename, approximate date, event, people, and review status potentially helpful fields. They do not require every field to be filled for every file. If a date is an estimate, the record should say so. They also want to keep track of whether an image came from an original camera file, a scan, or an edited copy when that is known. Nobody has decided whether to keep both TIFF and JPEG versions of a scan, so that choice should be discussed rather than silently settled.
4. Access is limited to Mara, Eli, and June for now. They sometimes share selected pictures with cousins, but the full archive is not intended to be broadly shared. Mara said, “I want the family to be able to find things, not to turn this into a public album.” If a future sharing method is mentioned, it should be distinguished from the present archive arrangement. The relatives have not agreed on one person being solely responsible for every future update.

Mara’s current draft of the local settings is:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 56
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"

The number of days is a starting value Mara copied from an example, not a decision the family has reviewed. She wants the planning assistant to explain what questions they should resolve before treating it as the retention period. Her notes do not specify which file versions should count toward retention, whether the setting refers to deleted files or all files, or how a restore would work. Those details remain open. The family has not asked anyone to implement the configuration, and Mara wants the recommendation to identify assumptions rather than present unresolved choices as settled.

At a Sunday visit, June brought out a paper envelope marked “Grandpa’s garden” and recognized several people in the prints, including her cousin Ruth and Mara’s father, Peter. She said, “That was before the fence went up, so it might help us place the pictures, but I can’t give you a year.” Mara scanned the envelope’s label and wrote down the names, but has not scanned the prints. The photos show a small greenhouse, a striped deck chair, and a row of tomato plants; the family thinks the garden was behind June’s first house. They do not know whether any of those prints overlap with images on the drives. This is one example of why they want source and review notes to stay with uncertain material.

The family hopes to begin with a usable local archive and a repeatable routine, then revisit decisions after they know the collection size and have tested the process on a small batch. Mara is comfortable following a short sequence of steps, while Eli prefers to see the reasoning behind choices that could affect original files. June’s recollections may add context over time, but the plan should not depend on getting every date and name from her before work can begin. The planning assistant should use these circumstances to shape recommendations for this specific family, including a practical way to keep track of what has been copied, checked, and left for later review.", "output": "Create a practical prompt for a planning assistant to recommend settings and a weekly intake routine for the Calder family’s photo archive, using the reference notes below.
